To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

correcting for putative biases in the US population yielded substantial increases in all- cause mortality hazard ratios for obesity that corresponded to substantial increases in excess deaths attributable to this disorder.

correcting for regression-dilution bias and for the reverse-causality bias increases the all-cause mortality hazard ratio for obesity from 1.26 to 1.66 and to 2.71, respectively, and that correcting for these biases increases the estimated number of excess deaths attributable annually to obesity in the United States from 112 000 to 280 000 and 470 000, respectively.
correcting for putative biases in estimating excess deaths attributable to overweight and obesity in the US yielded substantial increases in all-see mortality hazard ratios for obesity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the putative biases in the estimation of mortality attributable to obesity.
the putative biases in estimating the excess mortality attributable to obesity.
the effects of correcting two putative biases on the estimates of deaths attributable obesity in the US, using a large cohort.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the true excess deaths attributable to overweight and obesity are probably somewhere between the lower estimates of the previous analysis and the upper estimates of the present one.
obesity is a major cause of death and that the number of excess deaths attributable is much larger than previously believed.
obesity is a major contributor to excess deaths in the US.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the putative biases in estimating excess deaths attributable to overweight and obesity are real and substantial.
correcting for putative biases in estimating the mortality risk associated with obesity in the US may yield substantial increases in estimates for excess deaths attributable to this condition.
the putative biases in estimating excess deaths attributable to overweight/obesity in the US population are not trivial.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider the effects of regression dilution and reverse causation when estimating the effects of obesity on all-cause mortality.
the putative biases may have contributed to underestimating the excess deaths attributable to excess weight in the US population, and that further research is needed to correct for them.
it is not presently known how many excess deaths are attributable to obesity in US adults.
